passages.t: The LORD calls from the tent
passages.happening:
“Then the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting” (verse 1).

He tells Moses what to say to the people: “When any of you brings an offering to the LORD, you may bring as your offering an animal from the herd or the flock” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Exodus ended with a problem. The tent had been set up, the glory of the LORD had filled it, and “Moses was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting” (Exodus 40:35). Leviticus opens at that very moment. God speaks from inside the tent to the man standing outside it, and begins to explain how people may come near.

The Hebrew name of the book is Vayikra, ‘and he called’, from its first word. God makes the first move. Nothing in what follows is Israel's own plan for reaching God or winning him over. He calls, he speaks, and he gives the way.

The words are for everyone. ‘Speak to the Israelites’ means that these are not secrets kept by priests. Any Israelite may bring an offering, and every Israelite is told how.

The Hebrew word for ‘offering’ is qorban. It comes from the verb ‘to come near’. An offering is something brought near, and the one who brings it comes near with it. The first seven chapters describe five kinds of offering. This chapter begins with the oldest and most common, the burnt offering.

One more thing should be noticed. These laws come after the rescue from Egypt, not before it. Israel does not bring offerings in order to become God's people. It brings them because it already is.
passages.later:
The end of Exodus sets the scene: “Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34).

The word qorban appears once in the New Testament, in its Hebrew form. Jesus rebukes people who declared their goods ‘Corban’, a gift devoted to God, so that they would not have to support their parents (Mark 7:11).

The letter to the Hebrews invites its readers to do what this book teaches Israel to do: “let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:22).
passages.asks: God spoke first, from the tent, to a people who could not come in. Ask whether you think of coming to God as something you must work out for yourself, or as an answer to a call. And ask what it means to you that he wants people near.

passages.t: A burnt offering from the herd
passages.happening:
“If one’s offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he is to present an unblemished male. He must bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD” (verse 3).

“He is to lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him” (verse 4).

The worshiper kills the young bull himself. The priests, Aaron's sons, bring the blood and sprinkle it on all sides of the altar (verse 5). The worshiper skins the animal and cuts it into pieces. The priests lay the pieces on the wood of the altar fire, and the inner parts and legs are washed (verses 6-9).

Then “the priest shall burn all of it on the altar as a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
What made this offering different from every other is one word in verse 9: all. The whole animal went up in smoke. The worshiper ate none of it, and the priest kept only the hide (7:8). The Hebrew name, olah, comes from the verb ‘to go up’. It was a gift with nothing held back.

The worshiper did much of the work with his own hands. He chose a bull from his own herd, a costly animal. He brought it to the entrance of the tent, laid his hand on its head, and killed it. He skinned it and cut it up. The priests did only what belonged to the altar: the blood, the fire and the arranging of the pieces. Worship in Israel was not something to watch.

The animal had to be ‘unblemished’. The Hebrew word, tamim, means whole or complete. God was not to be given what was flawed or left over.

What did it mean to lay a hand on the animal's head? Readers have understood it in more than one way. Some see it as a sign of ownership: this gift is truly mine. Others see the animal standing in the worshiper's place. The verse itself says what it achieved: the offering was ‘accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him’. Even this offering, which was mostly an act of devotion, admitted that a person does not simply walk into the presence of God.

‘A pleasing aroma’ does not mean that God was hungry. In the Babylonian flood stories the gods go hungry when sacrifices stop, and crowd around the first one like flies. Israel's Scriptures say the opposite. The phrase means that God accepts the gift.

Burnt offerings were ancient long before Sinai. Noah offered them after the flood, and Job offered them for his children. Later, at the temple in Jerusalem, one was offered for the whole nation every morning and every evening, until the temple was destroyed in AD 70.
passages.later:
The phrase ‘pleasing aroma’ first appears after the flood: “Then Noah built an altar to the LORD”, and “the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma” (Genesis 8:20-21).

A psalm makes plain that God does not need to be fed: “Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Psalm 50:13).

The prophet Malachi later rebuked people who brought damaged animals: “When you offer blind animals for sacrifice, is it not wrong?” (Malachi 1:8).

The New Testament draws its own line from this offering to Jesus. Paul writes that Christ “gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God” (Ephesians 5:2). Peter speaks of “the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). That line is the New Testament's own. It does not make Israel's worship empty. As the notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real, and God truly accepted the offerings he commanded.
passages.hard:
Why would God want animals killed and burned?

To many modern readers animal sacrifice seems cruel or primitive, and the question deserves a plain answer. It helps first to see what the text does not say. It does not say that God needs food, or that his favor can be bought. Sacrifice in Leviticus is a costly gift from a people already rescued. It was a way of confessing that life belongs to God, and it was the means God himself gave for sinners to come near him.

Interpreters stress different sides of it. Some stress the gift: the worshiper gives something of real value, and gives all of it. Others stress that the animal's life is given in place of the worshiper's, with death faced as the cost of sin (17:11). Others stress the shared meal, which is clearer in chapter 3.

Israel's prophets insisted that sacrifice without justice and a humble heart was worth nothing. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Psalm 51:17). But they did not abolish the altar.

Christians believe that the sacrifices were fulfilled and ended in Christ's one offering of himself (Hebrews 10:1-18). Judaism has lived without animal sacrifice since the temple was destroyed in AD 70, and understands prayer, study and acts of kindness as carrying it on.
passages.asks: The burnt offering kept nothing back for the one who brought it. Paul asks Christians “to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1). Ask what part of your life you hold back from God. And ask what it would mean to give him something and keep none of it.

passages.t: A burnt offering from the flock
passages.happening:
“If, however, one’s offering is a burnt offering from the flock”, from the sheep or goats, “he is to present an unblemished male” (verse 10).

He kills it on the north side of the altar. The priests sprinkle its blood against the altar on all sides (verse 11). The animal is cut up, its inner parts and legs are washed, and the priest burns all of it: “it is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
This is the same offering in a smaller size. A bull was a rich family's gift. A sheep or a goat was within reach of many more households.

The steps are the same as before, and the passage ends with the same words. That repeating is how the chapter teaches. Whether a worshiper brings a bull or a goat, the offering is called by the same name and meets the same welcome.

Only one detail is new: the animal is killed on the north side of the altar. The text gives no reason for it, and none should be invented. The chapter is laying out an ordered way of worship in which each thing has its place.
passages.later:
Abraham had once been asked for a burnt offering he could hardly bear to give. On the way up the mountain he said, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son” (Genesis 22:8), and God provided a ram in Isaac's place (Genesis 22:13).

John the Baptist used the picture of a lamb when he saw Jesus: “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).
passages.asks: The same words of acceptance are spoken over the goat as over the bull. Ask whether you measure what you bring to God against what others bring. And ask whether you believe that a smaller gift, honestly given, is received as gladly.

passages.happening:
“If, instead, one’s offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon” (verse 14).

Here the priest does the work. He brings the bird to the altar, wrings off its head, and drains its blood on the side of the altar (verse 15). He removes the crop and throws it on the ash heap, and tears the bird open by its wings without pulling it apart (verses 16-17).

“And the priest is to burn it on the altar atop the burning wood. It is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
A single bird cost very little. Almost anyone could bring one. The law does not say in so many words that the birds are for the poor, but Leviticus says it elsewhere: a person who ‘cannot afford a lamb’ may bring two birds (5:7; 12:8).

The bird is too small for the worshiper to kill, skin and divide, so the priest handles it for him. The rite is made to fit what the person is able to bring.

And the last line is the same as for the bull: ‘a pleasing aroma to the LORD’. The chapter has walked down from the most costly gift to the least, and the ending has not changed. No one in Israel was too poor to come near to God with a whole gift.
passages.later:
When Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple, they offered “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24). It was the offering of people who could not afford a lamb.

Jesus once watched a poor widow put two small coins into the temple treasury and said, “this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury” (Mark 12:43).
passages.asks: God made a way for the person with almost nothing to bring a whole offering. Ask whether you have ever felt you had too little to give God: too little money, time, strength or faith. And ask whom you may have treated as though their small gift mattered less than a large one.
